questions.q: Why does mapping account or subscription boundaries directly onto the org chart (one per team or department) tend to fail?
options: An org chart describes who reports to whom, not what should fail together, so boundaries have to be redrawn on every reorg and are often the wrong size in both directions at once
Org charts never have more than two levels, so there aren't enough boundaries to create
Cloud providers technically forbid naming an account after a department
It fails only because it costs more money than any other approach
questions.explain: The guide's core argument: reporting structure and risk/blast-radius are different things, so an org-chart-shaped boundary is both too coarse (mixing risky and low-stakes workloads under one team) and too fine (splitting workloads that should share a boundary) at once, and it shifts every time people move teams.

questions.q: What is the actual design question blast radius asks you to answer when deciding on an account or subscription boundary?
options: Which team currently owns the budget line for this workload?
If this one account or subscription were fully compromised, misconfigured, or hit a hard limit, what's the worst case?
How many engineers are assigned to this project this quarter?
Which region was this workload originally deployed in?
questions.explain: Blast radius reframes the decision as a risk calculation: the boundary should contain the largest worst-case the organization is willing to tolerate from a single incident.

questions.q: Which of these is explicitly named in the lesson as one of the four dimensions that should drive an account/subscription boundary decision?
options: The programming language the workload's codebase is written in
Compliance/regulatory scope — keeping a regulated workload's audit boundary small and specific
The physical office location of the team that built the workload
The color scheme used in the team's internal dashboards
questions.explain: The four dimensions named are security blast radius, compliance/regulatory scope, billing/cost isolation, and operational access — compliance scope is one of them.

questions.q: What is the problem with the 'one shared account for everything' anti-pattern?
options: It is actually the recommended approach for any organization with fewer than ten employees
It makes subscription vending and Account Factory automation technically impossible to configure
It has no downside as long as IAM permissions are configured carefully

It ignores blast radius in the opposite direction from org-chart mirroring — a single mistake or compromised credential anywhere in that account has a blast radius equal to the entire company's cloud footprint
questions.explain: One shared account is the opposite mistake from one-account-per-team, but with the same root cause: it ignores blast radius, just by making every boundary as large as possible instead of as small as the org chart happens to dictate.

questions.q: How does the blast-radius framework from this lesson connect back to subscription vending (Lesson 6) and Account Factory (Lesson 7)?
options: It doesn't connect — blast radius is purely a manual, case-by-case human judgment call with no automation possible
It replaces subscription vending and Account Factory entirely with a new, separate tool

The framework becomes the decision logic inside the vending or Account Factory pipeline, so inputs like workload type and data sensitivity automatically determine which management group or OU a new subscription or account lands in
It only applies to Azure, not AWS, so it has no bearing on Account Factory
questions.explain: Whatever boundary framework an organization settles on becomes the actual deciding logic that the automated vending or Account Factory pipeline uses to place a new subscription or account, instead of a human deciding case by case.
